title: QCORE: A Quantum-Control-Oriented Real-Time Execution Architecture with Extensible Closed-Loop Services and Shared AI Acceleration
authors: Heyue Li, Yanshu Guo, Qichun Liu, Tiefu Li, Zhihua Wang, Hanjun Jiang
abstract: Scalable quantum processors require control, readout, feedback, calibration, and error correction to coexist under bounded latency and shared-resource constraints, whereas existing platforms typically optimize only a subset of these capabilities. This article presents QCORE (Quantum-Control-Oriented Real-Time Execution), a QPU-side digital control reference architecture positioned between the Host and a platform-specific analog/mixed-signal front end. QCORE separates task management, shared resources, hard-real-time execution, and long-timescale services into four hardware partitions. A fast-result sideband closes same-round feedback, a Measurement Packet provides a traceable measurement and service interface, and a common service-control skeleton, Tile-local QEC, and versioned safe-point commit organize calibration, error correction, and long-term state updates. Transaction-level, event-driven, and quantum-behavioral models are used for evaluation. At a background load of 0.8, the $P_{99}$ latency of the shared Measurement Packet/Event feedback path is $(1.984\pm0.004)L_{\max}$. Closed-loop operation reduces the mean frequency error by $83.2\%\pm0.8\%$ and lowers the state-assignment error at maximum readout drift from $10.39\%\pm0.54\%$ to $5.37\%\pm0.29\%$. No unsafe acceptance or mixed-version observation is observed in 100,000 configuration transactions, and Tile-local QEC reduces modeled global-boundary demand and yields a $2.08\times$ capacity-normalized scaling estimate.
summary: This paper introduces QCORE, a novel digital reference architecture designed to manage all necessary services—control, readout, calibration, and error correction—for scaling quantum processors. By partitioning tasks into dedicated hardware modules and enforcing strict versioning via safe-commit mechanisms, QCORE achieves superior real-time performance and reliability for complex quantum experiments.
main_problem: Scaling quantum processors requires integrating complex, concurrent control, readout, calibration, and error correction services under strict latency and shared-resource constraints.
main_result: The proposed QCORE architecture successfully unifies these disparate functions into a single digital reference boundary, demonstrating significant performance improvements in feedback latency and error reduction compared to existing systems.
method: The authors designed QCORE as a hardware-partitioned, real-time execution architecture that uses transaction-level and event-driven modeling to manage task admission, resource scheduling, and atomic state commits.
model_or_system: The system targets Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) utilizing transmon qubits. The control flow involves managing tasks through a Runtime Manager, executing sequences like Rabi-Ramsey calibration, and incorporating error correction codes (QEC).
key_observables: P99 latency of the feedback path ($\approx 1.984 L_{	ext{max}}$), reduction in mean frequency error ($83.2\%$), and state-assignment error reduction from $10.39\%$ to $5.37\%$.
important_parameters: Background load (e.g., 0.8), maximum readout drift, and the number of configuration transactions (100,000).
main_assumptions: Deterministic execution is defined behaviorally rather than by fixed RTL cycle latency; late or version-mismatched results cannot alter the current real-time state.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the QCORE architecture, comparing it to conventional control methods, and detail functional flows for calibration (Rabi-Ramsey) and Randomized Benchmarking (RB).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the limitations of existing quantum control systems, proposes the modular QCORE reference architecture with its four hardware partitions, details the execution flow through task management and resource scheduling, and validates performance using multiple complex workloads.
why_interesting: For AMO physicists working on open quantum systems, this work provides a crucial blueprint for the classical control infrastructure needed to reliably operate and characterize superconducting qubits in real-time, directly addressing hardware bottlenecks beyond the physics itself.
